name: Oku

tone_statements.citation: Akumbu, Pius W. & Roland Kießling. 2023. Variation in Central Ring: Convergence or divergence? Linguistic Typology at the Crossroads 3(1): 19-42. Bologna: University of Bologna. doi:10.6092/issn.2785-0943/16312
tone_statements.quote: As in the Ring and Momo sub-groups of Western Grassfields Bantu generally, noun class prefixes (NPx) in Central Ring languages have high tone underlyingly. [...] the high tone in Oku kə́-bân (1a) and Kom á-báyn (1b) contrasts with the low tone in Babanki cognate kə̀-báyn (1c). [...] In isolation, the high tone in these noun prefixes is generally lowered to mid, as is shown in Table 3 [...]. This is illustrated by the Oku (2a) and Kom (2b) examples where spreading of the NPx H creates HL falling contour tones on underlying L roots in both languages. Having spread to the root tone, the NPx H is then realized as M in isolation.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 23-24, §2.1 'Low tone in noun class prefixes', with ex. (1a), Table 3 and ex. (2a)
tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone language: noun roots fall into four tone classes (H and L roots each with a floating H or L: HH̥, HL̥, LH̥, LL̥); noun class prefixes underlyingly H, realized M in isolation, their H spreading onto L roots to give HL falling contours; surface H, M, L and HL falling (partial statement restricted to nominal tone; no TBU or verb-tone statement here).

tone_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2014. How to study a tone language, with exemplification from Oku (Grassfields Bantu, Cameroon). Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 525-562. hdl:10125/24624 (earlier version: UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 2010, doi:10.5070/P72TR4S97H)
tone_statements.quote: (25) a. surface contrasts i. three tone heights (H, M, L) ii. a level L˚ tone which contrasts with L only before pause iii. falling contours: HM, HL, ML iv. no rising contours, with one exception (ncìí ‘chief’s house’) … from the presence of HM, HL, and ML contours, it is obvious that Oku tone cannot be analyzed as privative. … I will now suggest that the underlying system is /H/ vs. /L/ in Oku, and that all M tones are derived, as is the contrast between L˚ and L.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 544-545, section 4 'Stage III: Developing a tonal analysis', summary (25a) and following paragraphs

sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2014. How to study a tone language, with exemplification from Oku (Grassfields Bantu, Cameroon). Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 525-562. hdl:10125/24624 (earlier version: UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 2010, doi:10.5070/P72TR4S97H)
sources.note: Nothing about stress in Oku (the only 'stress' mentions concern Corejuage in the appendix). Full tonal analysis of Oku from 1977 fieldnotes: surface H, M, L, L˚ before pause, falling contours HM/HL/ML, no rising contours; nouns mostly prefix+monosyllabic root with M (occasionally L, never H) prefixes; underlying /H/ vs /L/ with M derived (p.545-546).

tone.locator: pp. 544-545, section 4 'Stage III: Developing a tonal analysis', summary (25a) and following paragraphs
tone.says: Two underlying tones, /H/ vs /L/; surface H, M, L, a level L˚ and falling HM, HL, ML contours are derived by rule (M = H lowered after L); floating H and L tones; noun roots /H, L, HL, LH/.
